title: Profiling with pprof
summary: **pprof** is Go's built-in profiler. It samples your program while it runs — where it spends CPU, what allocates memory, which goroutines are blocked — and lets you view the result as flame graphs, call trees, or annotated source. It is the single most important tool for turning a 'this is slow' hunch into a precise, data-backed fix.

subtopics.title: CPU profiling
subtopics.explanation: A CPU profile samples the call stack ~100 times per second (the runtime sets SIGPROF). After collection, pprof tells you which functions were *on-CPU* most often — i.e. where wall-clock time is actually spent. It measures running code, not time spent blocked or sleeping.

subtopics.title: Heap & allocation profiles
subtopics.explanation: The heap profile is a sampled snapshot of live (in-use) memory; the alloc profile counts total bytes/objects ever allocated. Use inuse_space to find leaks and live bloat, alloc_space to find allocation churn that pressures the garbage collector.

subtopics.title: net/http/pprof for live services
subtopics.explanation: Importing _ "net/http/pprof" registers debug handlers under /debug/pprof/ on the default mux. You can then pull a 30s CPU profile or a heap snapshot from a *running* production server without restarting it.

subtopics.title: runtime/pprof for programmatic capture
subtopics.explanation: For binaries that aren't HTTP servers (CLIs, batch jobs), use runtime/pprof to start/stop a CPU profile or write a heap profile from inside main(). This gives you exact control over the profiling window.

subtopics.title: Reading the output (flat vs cum, flame graphs)
subtopics.explanation: In pprof, *flat* is time spent inside a function itself; *cum* (cumulative) includes everything it called. Flame graphs visualise the call tree where width = time. Widest frames are your hotspots; follow them down to the self-time leaf.

subtopics.title: Block & mutex profiles
subtopics.explanation: The block profile records time goroutines spend blocked on synchronization (channels, mutexes); the mutex profile records contention on locks. Both must be explicitly enabled with a sampling rate before they record anything.

foundations.overview: Optimizing by guessing is how engineers waste days speeding up code that was never the bottleneck. pprof removes the guessing: it is a sampling profiler built into the Go runtime that records, with low overhead, where your program actually spends CPU, where it allocates memory, and where goroutines block. You collect a profile, open it with `go tool pprof`, and the data points you straight at the few functions that matter.
foundations.formalDefinition: pprof is a statistical (sampling) profiler and a suite of tooling: the runtime collects periodic stack-trace samples for CPU, memory, blocking, and mutex events, writes them in the protobuf-based profile.proto format, and `go tool pprof` analyzes and visualizes them.
foundations.whyItMatters: Performance work without a profiler is folklore. pprof gives you evidence, so you optimize the 5% of code that costs 95% of the time — and you can prove the win afterward by comparing profiles. It is also the primary tool for diagnosing memory leaks and goroutine leaks in production.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of pprof as a camera with a fast shutter pointed at your call stack. It doesn't film every instruction; it takes thousands of snapshots. Functions caught in many snapshots are where the time goes — exactly like a long-exposure photo shows the busiest paths as the brightest streaks.
foundations.runtimePerspective: For CPU profiles the runtime arms an OS timer that delivers SIGPROF ~100 times/sec; the handler records the current goroutine's stack. Memory profiles hook the allocator, sampling roughly one allocation per 512KB by default (MemProfileRate). Because it samples rather than instruments every call, overhead is typically a few percent — low enough to run in production.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Cutting p99 latency in an API server, finding the allocation hot loop that's driving GC CPU up, diagnosing why a batch job got 2x slower after a refactor, and locating goroutine leaks via the goroutine profile.
foundations.businessImpact: Profiling-driven optimization routinely cuts CPU or memory in half, which directly reduces the number of machines a service needs — a measurable cloud-bill reduction at scale.
foundations.engineeringImpact: It replaces opinion-driven optimization with data, so reviews focus on real hotspots; profiles attached to PRs make performance claims verifiable.
foundations.performanceImpact: CPU profiling adds only a few percent overhead and can run continuously in production with tools like continuous profiling; the insight it provides almost always pays for itself many times over.
commonUseCases: Finding CPU hotspots in a hot request path
Diagnosing memory leaks with inuse_space heap profiles
Reducing GC pressure by killing allocation churn (alloc_space)
Locating goroutine leaks via the goroutine profile
Investigating lock contention with mutex/block profiles

commonMisconceptions.myth: A CPU profile shows total time spent in each function, including waiting.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It only counts on-CPU time. A function blocked on I/O or a channel barely shows up — use block/goroutine profiles for that.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The heap profile shows every allocation.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It's sampled (one per ~512KB by default). It's statistically representative, not a complete ledger; adjust runtime.MemProfileRate for finer detail.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Profiling is too expensive for production.
commonMisconceptions.reality: CPU profiling adds only single-digit percent overhead and is routinely run live; many shops do continuous profiling.

visualExplorer.title: How a CPU profile is captured
visualExplorer.caption: From arming the timer to a flame graph, step by step.

config.intro: What happens when you collect a CPU profile:

steps.name: Start profiling
steps.detail: StartCPUProfile (or net/http/pprof) arms an OS timer that fires SIGPROF ~100 times per second.

steps.name: Sample the stack
steps.detail: On each SIGPROF, the runtime records the call stack of the goroutine that was running on that thread.

steps.name: Aggregate
steps.detail: Samples with the same stack are counted together — frequently-seen stacks accumulate the most samples.

steps.name: Write profile
steps.detail: On stop, the counts are written as a profile.proto file (cpu.out).

steps.name: Analyze
steps.detail: `go tool pprof` turns counts into flat/cum tables, call graphs, and flame graphs where width = time.

visualExplorer.title: Why CPU profiles only see on-CPU goroutines
visualExplorer.caption: SIGPROF samples whatever goroutine is currently executing on a thread (M). Goroutines parked off-CPU (blocked, waiting) aren't sampled — which is why blocking shows up in block/goroutine profiles, not the CPU profile.

interactiveExamples.title: The pprof workflow on the command line
interactiveExamples.explanation: These are the commands you actually type. Collect a profile, then explore it: `top` ranks functions, `list <fn>` shows annotated source, and `-http` launches the interactive flame-graph UI in your browser.

code.code:
# Collect a 30s CPU profile from a live server
go tool pprof http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30

# Or profile a benchmark and open the flame graph UI
go test -cpuprofile cpu.out -bench=BenchmarkParse .
go tool pprof -http=:8080 cpu.out

# Heap (in-use memory) snapshot from a live server
go tool pprof http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/heap

# Inside the interactive pprof prompt:
#   top 10              -> 10 hottest functions by flat time
#   list parseToken     -> annotated source for that function
#   web                 -> render a call graph (needs graphviz)

checkpoints.prompt: Your handler spends most of its wall-clock time waiting on a slow database call. Which profile will best reveal that?
options: The goroutine/block profile (and tracing), not the CPU profile
checkpoints.explanation: A CPU profile only samples goroutines that are running on a CPU. A goroutine blocked on a network read is off-CPU and barely appears. The goroutine profile (or block profile / execution tracer) shows where time is spent waiting.

checkpoints.prompt: In `go tool pprof`, what is the difference between a function's *flat* and *cum* time?
checkpoints.code:
(pprof) top
      flat  flat%   cum   cum%
     0.05s   2%    1.90s  90%  encoding/json.Marshal
options: flat is wall-clock, cum is CPU time
flat is time inside the function itself; cum includes time in everything it called
flat is the first sample, cum is the last
checkpoints.explanation: flat is self-time spent executing the function's own instructions; cum (cumulative) adds the time spent in all functions it called. A function with low flat but high cum is mostly a dispatcher — the real cost is in its callees.

checkpoints.prompt: This program means to write a CPU profile, but profile.out is empty/useless. Why?
checkpoints.code:
f, _ := os.Create("profile.out")
pprof.StartCPUProfile(f)
doExpensiveWork()
// program returns here
f.Close()
options: StopCPUProfile is never called, so buffered samples are never flushed
doExpensiveWork must run in a goroutine
checkpoints.explanation: StartCPUProfile must be paired with StopCPUProfile, which stops sampling and flushes the collected samples to the writer. Without it, the profile is incomplete or empty. The idiom is `defer pprof.StopCPUProfile()` right after StartCPUProfile.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the command to capture a 30-second CPU profile from a running service exposing net/http/pprof.
checkpoints.explanation: The /debug/pprof/profile endpoint collects a CPU profile; the seconds query parameter sets the duration. /heap and /goroutine return memory and goroutine snapshots respectively, and /metrics is Prometheus, not pprof.

codeLab.title: Kill allocation churn in a hot function
codeLab.instructions: Refactor `Join(parts []string, sep string)` so it produces the same string with far fewer heap allocations. The naive version concatenates with + in a loop (one new string per iteration). Use strings.Builder with a pre-sized buffer. The test asserts correctness AND that you allocate at most 2 times via testing.AllocsPerRun.
codeLab.expectedOutput: PASS  (ok  solution  0.01s)  — run `go test -bench . -benchmem` to see allocs/op drop from ~5 to ~1
hints: Each `out += p` allocates a brand-new string and copies everything so far — that's O(n) allocations.
strings.Builder appends into a growable byte buffer and only allocates when it needs more room.
Call b.Grow(n) with the exact final length so the buffer is allocated exactly once.
Profile it: `go test -bench=Join -memprofile=mem.out` then `go tool pprof -sample_index=alloc_space mem.out`.

debuggingLab.title: The profile is empty
debuggingLab.symptom: `go tool pprof cpu.out` reports 'Total samples = 0' even though the program clearly did work.

brokenCode.code:
func main() {
	f, _ := os.Create("cpu.out")
	defer f.Close()
	doExpensiveWork()        // all the work happens here...
	pprof.StartCPUProfile(f) // ...but profiling starts AFTER it
	defer pprof.StopCPUProfile()
}

debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Profiling only records samples between StartCPUProfile and StopCPUProfile. Here all the expensive work runs before StartCPUProfile, so by the time sampling begins there is nothing left to do. The defers also mean StopCPUProfile runs at the very end, but the window is still empty of real work.
commonMistakes: Starting the profiler after the code you wanted to measure.
Profiling a window so short that few or no SIGPROF samples land.
Forgetting that a sampling profiler needs the work to run *during* the window.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Move StartCPUProfile (and the defer Stop) above the work so the expensive code runs inside the profiling window.

solution.code:
func main() {
	f, _ := os.Create("cpu.out")
	defer f.Close()
	pprof.StartCPUProfile(f)     // start sampling FIRST
	defer pprof.StopCPUProfile()
	doExpensiveWork()            // now this runs inside the window
}

theory.question: What kinds of profiles does pprof support, and when would you reach for each?
theory.directAnswer: CPU (where on-CPU time goes), heap (live/in-use memory via inuse_space, and total allocations via alloc_space), goroutine (stacks of all goroutines — great for leaks), block (time blocked on synchronization), and mutex (lock contention). You reach for CPU for compute hotspots, heap for memory bloat and leaks, alloc_space for GC pressure, goroutine for leaks, and block/mutex for contention.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A family of sampled profiles produced by the runtime in the common profile.proto format.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Different performance problems live in different dimensions — CPU, memory, blocking — so each needs its own lens.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: CPU uses a SIGPROF timer; heap hooks the allocator with a sampling rate; block/mutex must be enabled with a sampling rate; goroutine walks all current stacks.

theory.whyImportant: Picking the wrong profile wastes time; knowing which one answers which question is the core skill.
theory.realWorldExample: Rising memory + flat CPU points you at the heap (inuse_space) profile; high CPU in GC points you at alloc_space to find churn.

followUps.question: Why doesn't a slow database call show up in a CPU profile?
followUps.answer: Because the goroutine is blocked off-CPU during the call; CPU profiles only sample running goroutines. Use the block/goroutine profile or the execution tracer.

followUps.question: What's the difference between inuse_space and alloc_space?
followUps.answer: inuse_space is memory currently live (find leaks/bloat); alloc_space is cumulative bytes ever allocated (find churn driving GC).

theory.question: How does Go's CPU profiler work, and why is its overhead low enough for production?
theory.directAnswer: It's a sampling profiler. The runtime arms an OS interval timer that delivers SIGPROF ~100 times per second; the signal handler records the stack of the goroutine running on that thread. Because it samples ~100 stacks/sec rather than instrumenting every call, overhead is just a few percent — low enough to run on live traffic.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Statistical sampling of call stacks driven by a periodic signal.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Full instrumentation would be far too slow; sampling gives statistically accurate hotspots cheaply.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: SIGPROF fires at the profile rate; the handler unwinds the current stack and increments a counter for that stack; counts are written as profile.proto on stop.

theory.whyImportant: Understanding sampling explains both why pprof is cheap and why short or rare events can be missed.
theory.realWorldExample: Continuous profilers (e.g. Pyroscope, Google Cloud Profiler) keep CPU profiling on permanently in production at negligible cost.

followUps.question: What's the default sample rate and can you change it?
followUps.answer: ~100Hz for CPU (runtime sets it); memory sampling is one per ~512KB via runtime.MemProfileRate, which you can lower for more detail.

followUps.question: Why might a hot but very short function be under-counted?
followUps.answer: Sampling can miss work that finishes between SIGPROF ticks; increasing the run time or sample rate improves accuracy.

scenario.question: A production API's CPU usage doubled after a deploy, but p99 latency is unchanged and no obvious code path looks slow. How do you find the cause with pprof?
scenario.directAnswer: Pull a 30s CPU profile from the live server via /debug/pprof/profile, open it with `go tool pprof -http`, and look at the flame graph and `top`. Doubled CPU with steady latency often means more work per request or GC overhead — so also pull a heap profile and check alloc_space for new allocation churn, and look for runtime.gcBgMarkWorker dominating the CPU profile. Compare against a profile from the previous release to spot the new hotspot.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A differential profiling investigation across two releases.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: CPU regressions are often allocation-driven (more GC) rather than a single slow function.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: pprof can diff two profiles (-base) to surface exactly what changed between releases.

scenario.whyImportant: Real regressions rarely announce themselves; profiling plus diffing localizes them fast.
scenario.realWorldExample: A new JSON-heavy code path quietly tripled allocations, pushing GC CPU up while per-request latency stayed flat.

followUps.question: How do you diff two profiles?
followUps.answer: go tool pprof -base=old.out new.out — positive nodes are the new cost introduced by the change.

followUps.question: How would you confirm it's GC?
followUps.answer: Look for runtime.gcBgMarkWorker / mallocgc in the CPU profile and check GODEBUG=gctrace=1 output for rising GC CPU.

coding.question: Write a small helper that profiles a CLI: it should start CPU profiling, run the program's work, and guarantee the profile is flushed even if the work panics. Implement `func WithCPUProfile(path string, work func()) error`.
coding.thoughtProcess: Create the output file, start the profile, and ensure StopCPUProfile + Close run no matter how work returns. defer handles both the normal and panic paths. Return early on file-creation errors. The key insight is that StopCPUProfile must be deferred so a panic in work still flushes the samples.
coding.lineByLine: os.Create opens the output file; we defer its Close. StartCPUProfile begins sampling and can fail if another profile is already running, so we check its error. The deferred StopCPUProfile is the crux: defers run during panic unwinding, so even a crash in work() still flushes a usable profile. work() runs inside the window, and we return nil on success.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) overhead beyond the cost of work itself.

followUps.question: How would you also capture a heap profile at the end?
followUps.answer: After work(), call runtime.GC() then pprof.Lookup("heap").WriteTo(f2, 0) to write an in-use heap snapshot.

followUps.question: Why defer StopCPUProfile instead of calling it at the end?
followUps.answer: So the profile is still flushed if work() panics or returns early; defers run during unwinding.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Expose net/http/pprof on a separate, access-controlled admin port — never on the public listener. In Kubernetes, scrape profiles via a sidecar or continuous-profiling agent so you have history when an incident hits.
productionDeepDive.performance: Profile representative load, not a toy benchmark. Use -base to diff releases. Optimize the widest flame-graph frames first; re-profile after each change to confirm the win and catch new hotspots you shifted the bottleneck onto.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: Goroutine and block profiles are your concurrency lenses: a goroutine profile with thousands of stacks stuck on the same line is a leak; the block profile reveals channels/locks where goroutines wait. Enable block/mutex profiling with a modest rate, since they aren't free.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Always pair StartCPUProfile with a deferred StopCPUProfile so crashes still flush data. Guard the pprof endpoints with auth — they expose stack traces and can be used to trigger expensive profiling as a DoS.
productionDeepDive.observability: Continuous profiling (Pyroscope, Parca, Google/Datadog profilers) keeps low-overhead CPU and heap profiles flowing so you can investigate after the fact and correlate with metrics and traces.
productionDeepDive.security: pprof endpoints leak internal symbol names and stack structure and let a caller make the server spend CPU collecting profiles. Bind them to localhost or an admin network and require authentication.

caseStudies.problem: Needed low-overhead profiling for production C++ and Go services.
caseStudies.solution: Sampling profiler writing a common protobuf format, analyzed by a shared tool.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Sampling trades completeness for tiny overhead; rare events can be missed.
caseStudies.lessons: A common profile format plus sampling makes always-on production profiling practical.

caseStudies.problem: CPU spikes in high-throughput Go edge services.
caseStudies.solution: Live CPU and heap profiles via net/http/pprof, diffed across releases.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Must secure the endpoints and profile under real load.
caseStudies.lessons: Most 'CPU regressions' turn out to be allocation churn driving the garbage collector.

keyTakeaways: pprof is Go's built-in sampling profiler: CPU, heap (inuse vs alloc), goroutine, block, and mutex profiles, all in one tooling.
CPU profiles only see on-CPU goroutines — blocking and waiting need goroutine/block profiles or the tracer.
Read flame graphs and `top` by flat (self) vs cum (including callees); optimize the widest frames and re-profile to prove the win.
Expose net/http/pprof for live services (on a secured admin port), and always pair StartCPUProfile with a deferred StopCPUProfile.
